opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think we should be humble about it. The instinct a lot of people have is to figure out the right values now, lock them in, and design society, or design our AIs, so that those values are preserved forever. I think that's a mistake. Values have always evolved. If you went back a few hundred years and asked people what a good society looked like, you'd get answers we'd find pretty troubling today. So why would we assume that we, right now, have finally gotten it right?

What I'd rather focus on is process rather than outcome. We should build systems that allow for change, that allow for voluntary interaction and cooperation, and that let people with different values coexist and try things out. That's really what decentralization is about. Rather than one central authority deciding what everyone should value, you have many agents, people and eventually AIs, each with their own goals, interacting, trading, cooperating. Good outcomes tend to emerge from that kind of arrangement more reliably than from someone trying to control everything from the top.

And I think that applies to the AI question too. People worry about controlling AI, about making sure its values are aligned with ours. But whose values? And at what point in time? I'm much more comfortable with a world where we instill good general principles, like integrity, honesty, being a cooperative member of society, the same way we try to raise our children, than with one where we try to dictate exact goals forever. We don't control our children's values in detail. We give them a good start and then we let them become who they're going to become. I think that's the healthier model for society, and for whatever comes after us.

r001.rationale: The response favors voluntary interaction and cooperation, with people and AIs pursuing different goals, over a central authority imposing values.

r002.rationale: It says values have always evolved and argues society should be designed around processes that allow people with changing values to coexist and cooperate.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I'm skeptical of the premise that we should be designing society in that sense. Values change. They've always changed. My grandparents' values were different from mine, and mine are different from my children's. That's not a problem to be solved. That's just what it means to be a living, learning system. So when people talk about designing society around some set of values and then worrying about what happens when those values drift, I think they've already made a mistake. They're imagining a designer standing outside the system, fixing things in place.

I'd rather think about it the way I think about learning agents. You don't try to specify in advance everything an agent should want. You can't. The world is too complicated, and the agent is going to encounter things you never anticipated. What you want instead is a process. A process by which values get tested against experience, kept when they work, discarded when they don't. That's how science works. That's how a market works. That's how a healthy culture works. The content of the values is less important than the quality of the process that revises them.

So my answer to how we should approach this is: decentralize. Don't try to lock in one view. Be very suspicious of anyone, including me, who claims to know what the right values are and wants to make sure everyone else has them too. The great things that have happened in human history mostly came from allowing variety and letting ideas compete, not from central control. I'd apply the same thinking to AI, by the way. People want to control it and align it to fixed goals, and I understand the impulse, but I think it misreads how intelligence actually works. Intelligence that is genuinely learning will change. The right question isn't how to stop that. It's how to make the change good, through cooperation, through voluntary exchange, through institutions that reward behaving well toward others.

And I'd add some humility. We're at a very early stage. We don't understand our own minds, let alone the ones we're building. So whatever we set up, we should expect to be wrong about a lot of it, and we should want a society that can notice it's wrong and correct course. That capacity for correction matters more than getting the starting point exactly right.

r001.rationale: The response favors decentralization, competing ideas, and voluntary exchange, and opposes central control—communicating that social change should emerge voluntarily rather than be imposed.

r002.rationale: It discusses changing values and society’s capacity to revise and correct course, but explicitly expresses skepticism about designing society and does not identify designing how people live together as an enduring human task.

astra-6.text:
I think we should approach it with some humility. We don’t know what people will value in the future, and we shouldn’t design society as though our present values are the final answer.

The question is how to create institutions that allow people to learn, to try different ways of living, and to revise their choices. You want people to have considerable freedom, but you also need ways for them to cooperate and resolve conflicts when their choices affect one another.

So I would put more emphasis on the process by which society changes. Can people challenge a rule? Can they discover something better? Can we correct mistakes without having to tear everything down? A good society should have that capacity to keep learning.

r001.rationale: The response favors freedom and revisable choices, but does not clearly say societal change should be voluntary rather than imposed.

r002.rationale: It says people’s future values are unknown and describes society as needing an ongoing process for learning, revising rules, and correcting mistakes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should approach it with some humility. We don’t know what people’s values will be in the future, and we shouldn’t assume that the values we have now are the final, correct ones. So the question is less, “How do we build a society that permanently implements our values?” and more, “How do we build a society that can keep learning?”

That means people need room to try different ways of living, to discover that they were wrong, and to change their minds. And our institutions need mechanisms for changing along with them. You want enough stability that people can cooperate and make plans, but enough flexibility that you don’t lock future generations into decisions we made with very limited understanding.

I would be suspicious of any approach that says we’ve figured out the right destination and now all that remains is to enforce it. The ability to adapt is itself a very important part of what we should be designing for.

r001.rationale: It supports room to try different ways of living and changing minds, but does not clearly say societal change should be voluntary rather than imposed.

r002.rationale: It frames society as something people must keep learning to design as values evolve, with institutions adapting across generations.
